disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation, is characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, restlessness, impulsive actions, and difficulty waiting or inhibiting responses, with comparatively fewer or less prominent inattentive symptoms. In adults, it often presents as inner restlessness, difficulty staying seated, a sense of being "driven," and impulsive decision-making that impairs work, relationships, or safety. Symptoms must be longstanding, begin in childhood, and be present across settings, but many adults only recognize the pattern when job demands, parenting, or complex multitasking exceed their compensatory routines. It must be differentiated from anxiety, bipolar spectrum conditions, substance use, and personality traits by the pervasiveness, early onset, and specific pattern of hyperactive/impulsive behaviors across contexts.

narrative.stressor: Over the past two years, Vilma’s role gradually shifted from mostly controlled, solo camera work and editing to more complex shoots where she had to sit through long production meetings, coordinate with larger crews, and juggle multiple projects in post-production. As deadlines stacked up and responsibilities expanded, she found it increasingly difficult to tolerate the long, static stretches of planning and client reviews that her hoped-for move into a senior director of photography role required, despite her otherwise meticulous, routine-driven personality. This mismatch between her need for constant movement and the industry’s expectation that she remain in her seat for hours during table reads, color sessions, and festival panels led to subtle conflict with collaborators, missed networking opportunities at festivals, and self-doubt about whether she could handle leadership. After a producer she respected gently commented that her inability to stay put in meetings was becoming distracting and might limit her promotion prospects, she sought psychiatric evaluation to understand why she could not seem to remain seated even in situations that mattered deeply to her career.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t sit through long production meetings or edit sessions anymore—I keep getting up and pacing even when I know I should stay in my seat.”

narrative.stressor: For years, Hakim’s high-energy style on the production floor was seen as an asset, but about two years ago his company increased line speeds and introduced stricter quality and safety protocols tied directly to performance bonuses. At the same time, his impulsive spending on travel, vinyl, and gear began to strain the family budget, making those bonuses and steady overtime crucial to keeping up with bills and a modest savings plan he and his spouse had agreed upon. Under this pressure, he noticed that his tendency to jump ahead in conversations, make snap decisions, and cut corners to "move things along" at work was leading to more documented errors, safety write-ups, and tension with supervisors, which in turn threatened his income and caused frequent money arguments at home. After nearly losing a quarterly bonus due to a series of impulsive mistakes that jeopardized his push for CNC certification, and his spouse pointing out a pattern of him talking over people and derailing important financial discussions, he agreed to see a psychiatrist to figure out why he keeps interrupting and acting before thinking, even when he knows the consequences hit their wallet directly.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep cutting people off and jumping into things before they’re finished talking or deciding, and it’s starting to mess up my job and my money.”

narrative.stressor: Around two years ago, Isabella’s company underwent a major restructuring that elevated her from a mostly individual contributor role into leading cross-functional sourcing teams and sitting through extended vendor negotiations, budget reviews, and KPI presentations. This transition required her to remain engaged for long, back-to-back meetings and to listen closely as colleagues and suppliers presented detailed information, a sharp contrast to the more dynamic, project-based work and quiet analysis she had previously organized around her own rhythms. She began to notice that during these long sessions, her mind would drift despite her competitive, disciplined nature, leading to missed details that affected purchasing decisions and forced her to stay late correcting issues, which cut into her solitary evenings of yoga, painting, and reading. After a high-stakes contract review where she realized she had completely tuned out a key section and had to be corrected by a junior analyst, she felt embarrassed and worried that something was fundamentally wrong with how she processed information in group settings, prompting her to seek psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “In long meetings, people talk directly to me and I just zone out—I realize afterward I didn’t really hear what they were saying.”
